source_reviews.independent_solution: The required learned categories are thermal effects, chemical effects and magnetic effects. Thermal effects include a resistive conductor warming when current transfers energy to it. Chemical effects mean a chemical change caused by current in a suitable conducting medium, such as electrode deposition or gas evolution in electrolysis; mere motion of the magnetic needle is not a chemical effect. Magnetic effects include a nearby magnetic needle turning, or a magnetic force between current-carrying conductors. The response must distinguish the three types, not replace them with the words battery, wire and switch. The wording 'can be observed' does not claim that every circuit necessarily displays all three effects simultaneously, and 'etc.' does not make these learned categories an exhaustive classification of every possible electrical phenomenon.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The teacher uses a low-voltage, current-limited demonstration circuit containing a power source, connecting wire and a switch; the depicted rheostat is part of the control apparatus. The magnetic needle can turn about its support, and the section of wire under discussion is placed above its axis, the line joining its two poles. Establish the original needle direction with the circuit open. On closing the circuit briefly, current in the wire generates a magnetic field that acts on the needle, which rotates away from its original position. On opening the circuit, that current ceases and its magnetic contribution is removed; the needle turns back to its original direction under the remaining background field. This does not mean that all magnetic fields vanish when the switch opens. The contrast between the two observations, with the apparatus otherwise unchanged, demonstrates the magnetic action of current on the needle. Students only observe and do not wire, touch the energized apparatus or use household circuits. Neither an exact angle, clockwise/counterclockwise direction nor a particular pole orientation can be inferred from the supplied prose and unlabelled needle. The actual image has an unresolved state-presentation defect: the switch is drawn and labelled open while the same scene carries a current arrow and a solid needle away from the stated dashed initial position. The text supplies the conditional sequence, but the static image must not be taken as evidence that an open steady circuit carries current.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Electric current is directed motion of charge in the chosen reference frame. A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field in the surrounding region, and that field can exert a magnetic turning action on a needle or forces on another current-carrying conductor. In the demonstration, the needle changes when current is switched on and returns when that current is removed, supporting attribution of the additional magnetic action to the current. Current is therefore called a source of magnetic field: 'the current's magnetic field' and 'the magnetic field produced by the current' express the same source relationship. This is not a claim that current is identical to the field, that an electric field is simply converted into a magnetic field, or that the needle creates the wire's field. Rest and motion must be compared in the same reference frame. For an isolated charge's own field in the elementary comparison here, a charge at rest supplies an electric field, whereas a moving charge has electric and magnetic field contributions. One must not transfer the single-charge statement to a claim that the total electric field of every neutral circuit is nonzero everywhere: positive and negative charges both contribute and can cancel. Similarly, saying a current produces a magnetic field in a region does not assert a nonzero resultant field at every point, exclude field superposition or imply that all background magnetism disappears when this current stops. No numerical law, field direction or field magnitude is required by the source task.

mathematics.independent_solution: A magnet can attract an iron nail by magnetic interaction. Like poles of two magnets repel; unlike poles attract in the elementary arrangement stated. A rubbed charged plastic comb attracting paper is an electrostatic interaction, caused by electrical charge and the response of the paper, not a magnetic attraction. Two parallel current-carrying wires exert magnetic forces on one another; current directions determine whether the force is attractive or repulsive, but d asks only whether a magnetic interaction exists. Therefore a, b and d are true, while c has the wrong force category and e has the wrong unlike-pole phenomenon.

mathematics.independent_solution: Directed charge motion constitutes the current in the observer's chosen frame. This current produces a magnetic field whether or not a magnetic needle is present. Electrical neutrality concerns net charge; it does not imply that oppositely charged carriers' velocity-weighted current contributions cancel. Since the stem stipulates a current, neutrality alone cannot establish zero magnetic contribution. Fields from other sources may coexist and superpose with the wire's own contribution. Stopping this current does not in general remove the other sources' fields. Thus d correctly explains the source relation, while a makes the detector into a source condition, b confuses charge neutrality with cancellation of current-generated magnetism, and c illegitimately assigns every nearby field to the wire.
